lesson.menu_desc: Tell me about a time you failed -- owning it, one regret, and what changed -- 33 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 15 -- The Failure Question
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Flavio Gattaz | Lesson 15 -- The Failure Question
lesson.grammar_point: expressing regret (wish and if only + past perfect, regret + -ing, regret to)

listenings.text: When I ask about a failure, I already know you have one, so I am not testing whether you will admit it. I am testing three things. The first is size. Candidates bring me a tiny failure, a typo in a report or a meeting that started late, because they think a small failure is a safe one. It is the opposite. If the failure was too small to hurt anybody, you have told me that nobody ever trusted you with anything that could go wrong. The second thing is ownership. I listen for the first time you say they, or the client, or the market. One sentence of context is fine. The moment you start shifting the blame, the answer is over, however good the rest of it is. And the third thing, the one that separates the strong answers from the rest, is evidence. Everybody tells me they learned something. Very few can tell me what they do differently now, on an ordinary Tuesday, because of it. A lesson with no change in behavior is a story, not a lesson. And please, do not dwell on it. Say the regret once, and then move on.

The first time somebody asked me for a failure, I gave the answer everybody gives. I said I worked too hard and trusted people too much, and I watched the interviewer stop writing. It was a strength wearing the clothes of a failure, and she had probably heard it forty times that week. The real failure was sitting right there and I did not use it. Two years earlier I had launched a product in a market we did not understand, and it fell short of the target by more than half. The second time I was asked, I owned up to it in the first sentence. I said the root cause was simple: I had never spoken to a single customer before we built it. I said I wished I had spent one week in that market instead of three months in meeting rooms. Then I stopped talking about the regret, and I described the rule we have now. Nobody signs off on a new product until they have interviewed ten customers personally. That rule was the real answer, not the failure.
